50.title: Five loaves and two fish (John 6:1–14)
50.hook: a boy hands over his lunch and five thousand are fed
50.carry: what you hand over is enough
50.howItsDone: Catholics read John 6 over several summer Sundays in the year of Mark, from the feeding on the hillside through the bread of life discourse, and hear it as pointing to the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Last week ended with the workers hired late, each paid the same denarius: grace isn't a wage. Now a new week: signs on the road. And it starts with a lunch.
screen: `GRACE ISN'T A WAGE.` → `WEEK EIGHT: SIGNS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: A hillside by the Sea of Galilee, near Passover, with much grass in the place, John says. A huge crowd has followed Jesus out here, thousands of people, a long way from any town. It's getting late. Everybody's hungry. Jesus turns to Philip, one of his disciples, and asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?" John adds that he asked this to test him, because he already knew what he would do. Philip counts the cost. Two hundred pence worth of bread, he says, wouldn't be enough for each of them to get a little. The need is enormous, and what they've got is nothing.
screen: `A HILLSIDE, A HUGE CROWD.` → `WHERE WILL WE BUY BREAD?` → `PHILIP COUNTS THE COST.`

segments.voice: Then Andrew speaks up, honest and a little embarrassed: "There is a boy here that hath five barley loaves, and two fishes; but what are these among so many?" John is the one who tells us it was a boy, and that the loaves were barley. Some readers note that barley bread was plain, everyday bread. This is a kid's packed lunch, and not a fancy one. Jesus says: make the people sit down. There's a lot of grass there, and the men sit down, about five thousand of them. Then Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. The Greek word for gave thanks is the root of a word Catholics know well: Eucharist. John's chapter six goes on, the next day, to Jesus calling himself the bread of life, and the Church reads this hillside meal as pointing toward the Mass. Then a detail that's easy to miss. When everyone's full, Jesus says: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost." They fill twelve baskets with leftovers. Nothing wasted, and more left over than they started with. In John's telling, it starts with a child who handed over what he had, even though everyone could see it wasn't enough.

segments.voice: Think of a need that seems too big, a friend's grief, a neighbor's struggle, a cause you care about, and of what you actually have. Not much: ten minutes, twenty dollars, one skill, a listening ear, five loaves and two fish. Choose one small thing you think won't matter and picture handing it over anyway; if you pray, you can offer it to God and let him do the rest.
Eucharist. The thanksgiving behind a boy's five loaves and two fish, feeding thousands with baskets of bread left over.
Your line: what you hand over is enough. Twelve baskets, from one small lunch. Day fifty, done.

51.title: Walking on the water (Matthew 14:22–33)
51.hook: Peter steps out, looks at the wind, sinks, and a hand catches him
51.howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass, and "Lord, save me" is used as a short prayer in hard moments; Peter's sinking and rescue is often preached as a picture of faith that falters and is caught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five loaves and two fish, the Eucharist's root, and a boy's lunch fed thousands. Your line was what you hand over is enough. That same night, the disciples are out on the lake.

After the crowd is fed, Jesus sends the disciples ahead across the lake by boat, and goes up a mountain alone to pray. Night falls. Out on the water, the wind is against them, and the boat is tossed by the waves. Then, in the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, they see someone walking toward them on the water. Matthew says they were troubled and cried out in fear: it's a ghost.
screen: `A HEADWIND ALL NIGHT.` → `THE FOURTH WATCH, BEFORE DAWN.` → `SOMEONE ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Jesus speaks at once, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be of good heart: it is I, fear ye not." It is I. In Greek, two words: egō eimi, I am. At the burning bush, in the old Greek translation of Exodus, God's name for himself begins with the same two words. Some readers hear that echo here. Then Peter, being Peter, says: Lord, if it's you, tell me to come to you on the water. Jesus says one word: come. Peter climbs over the side. And he walks. On the water. Toward Jesus. Matthew is the one who tells this part. Then, the text says, Peter saw the wind was strong, and he was afraid, and he began to sink. The wind hadn't changed; it had been strong all night. What changed was where Peter was looking. As he goes under, he prays: "Lord, save me." Three words. No speech. And immediately, Matthew says, Jesus stretched out his hand and caught him. The hand was already there. Then, gently: "O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?" Little faith, not no faith. Peter got out of the boat. The others didn't. They climb in, the wind stops, and the disciples bow down and say: truly, you are the Son of God. For Catholics, Peter matters especially. He's the one they call the first pope, the rock of the Church. And here the rock is sinking. The story doesn't hide it. It shows a leader who needed catching, and a hand that caught him.

If you pray, you can say Peter's three words, Lord, save me, and picture the hand reaching out; if not, just notice where you're looking, and try looking a little further up.

52.title: On the mountain (Matthew 17:1–8)
52.hook: Peter, James and John see him shining and want to stay up there
52.carry: you can't stay on the mountain
52.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Transfiguration on August 6, hear it on the Second Sunday of Lent, and pray it as the fourth Luminous Mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking on the water: egō eimi, it is I, and Peter sank, and was caught. Your line was the hand is already there. Today Peter is on a mountain, and he never wants to come down.

Think of a moment when everything was clear: a night under the stars, a wedding, the hour after a baby was born, a retreat where, for once, God felt close. You didn't want it to end; you wanted to build a little house right there and live in it. Jesus takes three friends, Peter, James and John, up a high mountain. And there, in front of them, something happens that they'll spend the rest of their lives trying to describe.
screen: `A MOMENT WHEN EVERYTHING WAS CLEAR.` → `THREE FRIENDS, A HIGH MOUNTAIN.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And he was transfigured before them. And his face did shine as the sun: and his garments became white as snow." The Greek word is metamorphōthē, the root of our word metamorphosis. His form changed. For a moment, the three see him as he is. And he's not alone. Moses and Elijah appear, talking with him: Moses, who gave the Law, and Elijah, the great prophet. The whole story of Israel, standing beside him. Peter, overwhelmed, says the most human thing in the chapter: "Lord, it is good for us to be here." If you want, he says, I'll make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah. Let's stay. Mark adds, kindly, that Peter didn't know what to say, because they were terrified. While he's still talking, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says what it said at the river on the day of the baptism, with three words more: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye him." Listen to him. The three fall on their faces in fear. Then Jesus comes, touches them, and says: arise, and fear not. They look up, and they see no one but Jesus alone. And they go back down the mountain, because down there is where the work is. The Church keeps the Transfiguration as a feast on August sixth, and reads this Gospel on the Second Sunday of Lent, a glimpse of the glory before the road to the cross. It's the fourth Luminous Mystery of the rosary. Tradition places it on Mount Tabor in Galilee; Matthew doesn't name the mountain.

segments.voice: Let one bright memory come back, a moment when things felt whole, or holy, or simply good, and without analyzing it, stand in it again and notice what it felt like in your body. Then notice that you came down from it, and you're still carrying something from it. If you pray, you can thank God for that moment.

53.title: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42)
53.hook: one sister serves and frets, the other sits at his feet, and one thing is necessary
53.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Martha, Mary and Lazarus each July, and religious communities often describe their life as holding Martha's work and Mary's prayer together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Transfiguration: three friends saw him shining. Your line was you can't stay on the mountain. Today, a kitchen.

Something's on the stove, the table isn't set, the bread needs cutting, and there's more to do than time to do it. Guests are here. In Luke's story the guest is Jesus, and a woman named Martha has welcomed him into her home. She's busy with all the serving. And her sister Mary? Sitting on the floor at Jesus's feet. Not helping. Just listening. Martha keeps glancing in, carrying plates, getting hotter by the minute. Finally she walks right into the room and says what she's been thinking.
screen: `SOMETHING'S ON THE STOVE.` → `MARTHA IN THE KITCHEN.` → `MARY ON THE FLOOR, LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Martha doesn't go to Mary. She goes to Jesus. Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me. It's the same question the disciples asked in the storm: don't you care? Jesus answers gently, saying her name twice, the way you speak to someone you love. In the Douay-Rheims: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary. Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." Careful here is old English for full of care. Luke's word means worry, anxiety. He doesn't say the serving is bad. He's saying: you're anxious about many things, and you're missing the one. And notice where Mary sits. At a teacher's feet is a student's place; in Acts, Paul says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. Mary takes the disciple's seat, and Jesus says it won't be taken from her. Some Christian writers, Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas Aquinas among them, read these sisters as two ways of life: the active and the contemplative, doing and praying. But the Church never throws Martha out. She's a saint, with her own feast day, now shared with Mary and their brother Lazarus. And in John's Gospel, it's Martha who makes a bold statement of faith. We'll hear her soon. Monks and nuns try to hold both sisters together: prayer and work, listening and serving.

segments.voice: Stop in the middle of a task, as you're doing now, in a way, and let the list in your head keep talking without answering it; just notice how many things are pulling at you. Then let them go quiet for a moment and sit where Mary sat. If you pray, just listen; if you don't, listen to the room, to your breath. One thing.

54.title: Up a tree (Luke 19:1–10)
54.hook: a short, rich, hated man climbs a sycamore and Jesus invites himself to dinner
54.carry: today salvation came to this house
54.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Zacchaeus at Sunday Mass and at the Mass for the dedication of a church, and it is often preached as a picture of welcome leading to conversion and restitution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha and Mary, the old word careful, and the line one thing is necessary. Today, a man in a hurry, running ahead to climb a tree.

Jericho. A crowd lines the street because Jesus is passing through. Somewhere at the back is a man named Zacchaeus. Luke gives us three facts about him. He's the chief of the tax collectors there. He's rich. And he's short. He wants to see Jesus, he can't see over anybody, and nobody is going to make room for him. So a grown man, wealthy and important, runs ahead down the road like a boy and climbs up into a sycamore tree. The neighbors are watching.
screen: `A CROWD IN JERICHO.` → `A TAX BOSS, RICH, AND SHORT.` → `A GROWN MAN CLIMBS A TREE.`

segments.voice: Jesus comes to the spot, looks up, and calls him by name. In the Douay-Rheims: "Zacheus, make haste and come down; for this day I must abide in thy house." He doesn't wait to be asked. He invites himself, and not to just anyone's house: to the house of the man the crowd calls a sinner. Zacchaeus scrambles down and welcomes him with joy. The crowd does not. Everyone grumbles: he's gone to stay with a sinner. Then Zacchaeus stands up and says something no one expected. Look, Lord, half of what I own I'm giving to the poor, and if I've cheated anyone of anything, I'll pay it back four times over. Notice the order. Jesus didn't make him promise first. He came to the house first. The welcome came before the change, and the change came pouring out of the welcome. Then Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house." And the line that sums up everything he's been doing on this road: "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." The sheep, the coin, the son, all in one sentence. One word ties it together: today. Luke used it at the birth, too: the angels say a savior is born to you this day. Now, in Jericho, today. Not someday, when you've fixed yourself. Today. The Church reads this Gospel when a new church building is dedicated: a house where Christ has come to stay.

segments.voice: Think of someone you've already made up your mind about: the difficult coworker, the neighbor with the loud truck, the relative who always says the wrong thing. You know what they're like, or you think you do. Hold them in mind, remember Zacchaeus called by name before he'd changed at all, and ask whether this person could still surprise you. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

55.title: Neither do I condemn thee (John 8:1–11)
55.hook: the crowd has stones, he writes in the dust, and they leave one by one
55.howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year C, and it is often preached before confession as a picture of mercy that frees a person and sends them into a new life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zacchaeus up a tree, and the line today salvation came to this house. Today, stones.

Early morning in the Temple courts. Jesus is sitting, teaching a crowd. Suddenly, a commotion. Some scribes and Pharisees push through, dragging a woman, and stand her in the middle of everyone. She's been caught, they say, in the act of adultery. Moses in the Law, they say, commanded such a one to be stoned. So what do you say? John tells us plainly it's a trap. If he says let her go, he's set aside the Law. If he says stone her, where's the mercy he's known for? Everyone waits. There are stones within reach. And Jesus doesn't answer. He bends down and starts writing on the ground with his finger.
screen: `A WOMAN DRAGGED INTO THE CROWD.` → `A TRAP.` → `HE WRITES IN THE DUST.`

segments.voice: What did he write? The Gospel never says. People have guessed ever since; some early Christian writers imagined he wrote the accusers' own sins in the dirt. But John leaves it blank, and it's honest to leave it blank too. They keep pressing him. So he straightens up and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he bends down and writes again. He doesn't stare them down. He gives them room. One by one they go away, John says, beginning with the eldest. Maybe they had the most to remember. Until it's just Jesus and the woman, still standing there. And where is the man? The Law they cite names both the man and the woman. The text is silent about him. Then Jesus looks up and speaks to her, maybe the first person all morning to speak to her rather than about her. Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you? No one, Lord. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Neither will I condemn thee. Go, and now sin no more." Both halves matter: no condemnation, and a new life. He doesn't pretend nothing happened, and he doesn't throw a stone. The Catholic Church receives this passage as sacred Scripture, part of John's Gospel, and reads it at Mass in Lent.

Then, if you want, turn the same mercy toward yourself, and if you pray, hear his words spoken to you.

56.title: Lazarus (John 11:1–44)
56.hook: four days in the tomb, Martha's faith, and the shortest verse, Jesus wept
56.howItsDone: Catholics hear the raising of Lazarus on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year A, and John 11 is one of the Gospels often chosen for funeral Masses, with its words, I am the resurrection and the life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crowd with stones, and neither do I condemn thee. Your line was go, and sin no more. Today, the last day of this week on the road, and it ends at a tomb.

A message arrives from two sisters we've met, Martha and Mary, in the village of Bethany. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." That's all it says. Their brother Lazarus, his friend. Jesus, John tells us, loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. And then he waits two more days before he goes. By the time he gets to Bethany, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. The house is full of mourners. Martha hears he's coming and goes out to meet him on the road. She doesn't say hello. She says what anyone would say.
screen: `HE WHOM THOU LOVEST IS SICK.` → `HE WAITS TWO DAYS.` → `FOUR DAYS IN THE TOMB.`

segments.voice: Martha says: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Grief and faith in one breath. Jesus answers: "I am the resurrection and the life." Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live. Do you believe this? And Martha, the busy sister from the kitchen, makes a bold statement of faith: Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God. Then Mary comes, falls at his feet, and says the very same words: Lord, if you had been here. She's weeping, the mourners with her are weeping, and Jesus, John says, is deeply moved and troubled. Where have you laid him? Come and see. And then: "And Jesus wept." A whole verse, three words; in Greek, too. John uses a different verb from the mourners' weeping: not wailing, but tears running down. He knows he's about to call Lazarus out. And he weeps anyway. Christians read in this that God doesn't skip past grief, even when the ending is already known. The people watching say: see how he loved him. At the tomb, Martha, practical to the end, warns him: Lord, by now there'll be a smell, it's been four days. They roll the stone away. Jesus prays, and cries with a loud voice: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man comes out, still wrapped in grave clothes. Unbind him, Jesus says, and let him go. This week: loaves, the water, the mountain, two sisters, a tree, the stones, and now a tomb.
